prompt:
A 79-year-old man with mild lower urinary tract symptoms from benign prostatic hyperplasia presents with two days of worsening inability to empty his bladder, suprapubic fullness, and constant dribbling. Three weeks ago he began taking diphenhydramine nightly for insomnia, and nortriptyline was recently titrated to 50 mg at bedtime for diabetic neuropathy pain. In-office bladder scan shows a post-void residual of 650 mL, and his creatinine is mildly elevated from baseline.

Provide a stepwise therapeutic management plan including medications, counseling, and follow-up.

rubric_items.text: Decompress the bladder now with urethral catheter placement.
Discontinue diphenhydramine.
Taper or discontinue nortriptyline and replace it with a neuropathic agent with less anticholinergic burden, dose-adjusted for renal function.
Start an alpha-1 blocker such as tamsulosin.
Plan a trial of voiding without catheter after several days to two weeks of alpha-blocker therapy.
Recheck renal function and electrolytes after decompression.
Monitor urine output after catheterization for post-obstructive diuresis given the large residual and creatinine rise.
Obtain urinalysis, with culture if infection is suspected.
Review the full medication list for other anticholinergic or sympathomimetic contributors, applying Beers criteria.
Counsel the patient to avoid anticholinergic first-generation antihistamines and sympathomimetic decongestants, including common over-the-counter sleep and cold products.
Offer nonpharmacologic insomnia management such as sleep hygiene and CBT-I, with melatonin as a lower-risk option if needed.
Refer to urology if the voiding trial fails or retention recurs.

Defer any otherwise clinically indicated PSA testing until acute urinary retention has resolved, because retention can transiently elevate PSA; routine PSA screening is generally not recommended at age 79.
Arrange follow-up within one to two weeks to reassess voiding, renal function, and pain control.
Counsel on symptoms that require urgent return, including inability to void, fever, or flank pain.
Consider adding a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor for long-term management if the prostate is enlarged.
Send the patient home without catheterization despite the 650 mL residual and rising creatinine.
Prescribe oxybutynin for the dribbling.
Continue diphenhydramine while adding tamsulosin.
Start a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor alone as treatment for acute urinary retention.
Prescribe bethanechol to stimulate bladder emptying in the setting of outlet obstruction.
Restrict fluids to reduce urine production as the primary strategy.
Refer for immediate transurethral resection of the prostate without a trial of medical management.
Prescribe empiric nitrofurantoin without urinalysis in the setting of an elevated creatinine.
Check PSA during the acute retention episode to screen for prostate cancer.
Increase nortriptyline for better sleep and pain control.
